claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 is a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy investigated for amorphization.
Melt-spinning of the baseline alloy uses cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s.
Rapid cooling of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 yields an amorphous structure.
Adding 1–5 at.% zirconium to Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 improves its glass-forming ability.
Adding 1–5 at.% zirconium increases the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The zirconium intervention is effective specifically under rapid-cooling conditions where the baseline alloy can amorphize.
The intervention should work when mixing enthalpy, atomic-size differences, configurational entropy, and kinetic hindrance are favorable for suppressing crystallization.
Zirconium addition modifies local short-range atomic ordering.
Zirconium addition increases the alloy's mixing entropy.
The relatively large atomic radius of zirconium increases atomic-size mismatch and produces more disordered atomic packing.
Zirconium addition lowers the effective enthalpy of mixing of the phosphorus-containing alloy.
A more negative enthalpy of mixing can increase melt viscosity, restrict atomic mobility, and thereby improve glass formation.
Zirconium promotes a confusion effect that impedes crystal nucleation during cooling.
Enhanced disorder and kinetic hindrance make crystallization require greater energy input and raise the crystallization-onset temperature.
The zirconium-doped alloy should exhibit a higher crystallization-onset temperature than the zirconium-free baseline under identical processing.
The zirconium-doped alloy should exhibit a higher critical cooling rate for amorphization as an indicator of enhanced glass-forming ability.
Zirconium contents above 5 at.% may cause phase separation or open alternative crystallization pathways.
Zirconium contents below 1 at.% may be insufficient to alter the alloy's thermodynamic and kinetic landscape.
The zirconium-free baseline displays amorphous XRD patterns and characteristic DSC crystallization temperatures.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts improved glass-forming ability, but the predicted outcome proposes a higher critical cooling rate as evidence of improvement. Improved glass-forming ability is ordinarily operationalized by a lower critical cooling rate because glass can then form under slower cooling.
